web_title: 7. Why the Price Is What It Is: Valuation, Reverse DCF & Peer Comps
book_title: Chapter 7: Why the Stock Trades Here — Market Expectations vs. Peers
question: At $37.99 ($56.43B market cap), what revenue growth and operating margin recovery is the market already pricing in—and how does NIKE stack up against Deckers, On Holding, Lululemon, Under Armour, and Dick's Sporting Goods?

epigraph.quote: Price is what you pay; value is what you get. When a former market darling de-rates by half, the trap is assuming the old multiple is the anchor rather than the new cash-flow reality.
epigraph.author: Institutional Valuation Principle

web_blocks.title: Deconstructing the $37.99 Share Price & Valuation Multiples

web_blocks.html: As of November 13, 2026, NIKE, Inc. (NKE) trades at $37.99, down 45.1% from its $69.14 52-week high and 18.8% above its $31.97 low [23]. Equity market cap is $56.43 billion and Finviz enterprise value is $59.13 billion (including lease obligations alongside $7.94B debt and $9.03B cash) [2, 23]. On trailing metrics, NKE looks modest: 18.21x trailing P/E ($2.09 TTM EPS), 1.23x Price-to-Sales, and 12.32x EV/EBITDA. It also carries a 4.32% trailing dividend yield ($1.64 TTM) [23].

Trailing multiples hide a crucial earnings bridge. NIKE's Forward P/E is 25.54x—a 40% premium to its trailing P/E. Why? FY2026 GAAP operating income ($3,789M) benefited from $986M in one-time IEEPA tariff recoveries [2]. Meanwhile, Q1 FY2027 EBIT fell 28% as Greater China dropped 26% (CC) and NIKE Direct slid 8% [3]. Consensus Q2 FY2027 EPS sits at $0.36–$0.38, implying ~$1.49 in forward EPS [23, 24]. The market is not pricing NKE as a distressed value stock; it is paying 25.5x forward earnings on faith that Elliott Hill restores double-digit margins [3, 23].

We run a 10-year Reverse DCF anchored to FY2026 revenue ($46,398M), a 9.0% WACC (Beta 1.03, ~4.2% risk-free rate, 5.0% ERP), and 3.0% terminal growth [2, 23]. Using ~1,485M diluted share equivalents ($56.43B / $37.99), the model tests what cash flows $37.99 already embeds:

web_blocks.caption: NKE Reverse DCF Sensitivity Matrix at $37.99 ($56.43B Market Cap, 9.0% WACC, 3.0% Terminal Growth)
web_blocks.takeaway: At $37.99, the market is already pricing in 3.5% annual revenue growth and an 11.5% terminal EBIT margin—meaningful improvement over FY2026's 8.2% GAAP EBIT margin (6.0% ex-tariff recovery) and Q1 FY2027's -1% top-line contraction.

web_blocks.html: The Reverse DCF exposes a tight margin of safety. At $37.99, investors do not get the turnaround for free. They already pay for 3.5% annual revenue growth and a +330 bps operating margin expansion to 11.5% (or +550 bps ex-tariff recovery) [2, 23]. If NKE stalls at 1.5% growth and an 8.5% EBIT margin, fair value drops toward $28. Reaching $45–$60 requires proving North America wholesale (+9%) can lift global growth back to 4.5%–6.0% and EBIT margins above 12.5% [3].

Historical multiple bands confirm this discipline. During 2015–2021, NKE commanded 26x–34x forward P/E and 2.8x–4.5x EV/Sales on high-single-digit growth. Today's 1.29x EV/Sales looks low, but on a 6.0% ex-tariff EBIT margin it equals ~21.5x EV/EBIT [2, 23]. In addition, FY2026 FCF ($2,184M) missed the $2,410M dividend by $226M [2]. Multiple expansion requires gross margins recovering above 45% and China stabilizing.

Share repurchases tell a similar capital-allocation story. During FY2017–FY2024, NIKE routinely retired shares using excess free cash flow. Today, management has dialed back net buybacks as operating cash flow tightened and inventory cleanup consumed working capital [2]. With $9.03 billion in cash and short-term investments against $7.94 billion in debt, liquidity is not at risk [2]. Still, equity buyers at $37.99 cannot count on aggressive buybacks to boost EPS until gross margins and working capital normalize.

What about sum-of-the-parts or franchise floor value? At $56.43 billion market cap, North America ($19.4B revenue) and EMEA ($12.1B revenue) alone account for roughly 68% of NIKE Brand sales [2]. Even valuing Converse ($1.5B revenue, -28% CC) at a steep discount, the core North America and EMEA franchises anchor the stock near $30–$32 in a bear case [2, 3]. Upside above $45, however, still hinges on Greater China stabilizing and wholesale gross margins holding firm.

Look also at the Wall Street consensus bridge into FY2028. At 25.54x forward P/E on $37.99, implied FY2027 EPS is roughly $1.49 [23]. Even if EPS rebounds +75% to ~$2.60 by FY2028–FY2029, the stock at $37.99 still trades at ~14.6x normalized future earnings two years out. That is reasonable, not dirt-cheap—confirming why patience for $33.50–$35.00 creates a real margin of safety.

web_blocks.caption: NKE vs. Global Athletic Footwear, Apparel & Retail Peers (Snapshot as of 2026-11-13)
web_blocks.takeaway: NKE trades at a steeper forward multiple (25.54x) than faster-growing, higher-margin peers Deckers (10.69x, 38.11% ROIC) and On Holding (16.47x, 24.02% TTM sales growth), underscoring how much turnaround recovery is already priced into NKE.

web_blocks.html: The peer matrix highlights NKE's valuation hurdle [23, 25, 26, 27, 28]. Deckers (DECK) earns a 23.47% operating margin and 38.11% ROIC at just 10.69x forward P/E [23, 25]. On Holding (ONON) grows sales 24.02% TTM with a 66.71% gross margin at 16.47x forward P/E [23, 26]. Even Lululemon (LULU) earns an 18.03% operating margin and 21.60% ROIC at 12.61x forward P/E [23, 27]. Paying 25.54x forward earnings for NKE (-1.36% TTM sales) assumes a rapid FY2028 margin snapback [23]. Meanwhile, Under Armour (UAA) at 0.43x P/S shows how far a broken athletic brand can fall [23, 28].

What Changes This Valuation Call: NKE shifts from expensive turnaround to undervalued value only if (a) price pulls back into the $33.50–$35.00 shelf (compressing EV/Sales toward ~1.15x) OR (b) Q2/Q3 FY2027 gross margins top 44.5% ex-tariff recoveries and lift consensus forward EPS above $2.30.

web_blocks.region_era: US Apparel & Footwear — Iconic Brand De-Rating Cycles
web_blocks.mechanism: When a legacy category leader over-rotates into lifestyle/fashion-cycle staples (e.g., VF Corp's Vans classic slip-on dependency) and stretches wholesale vs. DTC channel discipline, gross margins compress from markdowns and forward P/E stays optically elevated because consensus earnings fall faster than the share price.
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: VF Corp's revenue fell from $11.8B (FY22) to $10.5B (FY24) while operating margins compressed from >13% to <5%, forcing a 70% dividend cut in 2023 and a >75% peak-to-trough equity drawdown before restructuring took hold.
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: NIKE has a far stronger balance sheet (net cash ex-leases) than VF Corp ever had, so balance-sheet distress is not the risk. The risk is paying 25.5x trough forward earnings while the dividend ($2.41B) exceeds FCF ($2.18B) and China (-26% CC) has yet to bottom.

book_paragraphs: Now you and I finally lift the curtain on the stock price. For six chapters, we deliberately kept our eyes off the ticker tape so we wouldn't let a 45% drawdown trick us into calling a bruised turnaround a bargain—or scare us away from a great franchise at the bottom. On Friday, November 13, 2026, NIKE closed at $37.99 a share, giving the company a $56.43 billion equity market cap and a $59.13 billion enterprise value.

At first glance, a casual observer looks at NIKE's 18.2x trailing P/E, 1.23x Price-to-Sales, and 4.32% dividend yield and thinks, 'How can the Swoosh be cheap at 18 times earnings?' Stop right there. Look one line deeper at the forward multiple: 25.54x Forward P/E. Why is the forward P/E seven turns higher than the trailing P/E? Because FY2026 GAAP operating income of $3.79 billion was flattered by $986 million in one-time IEEPA tariff recoveries, and near-term earnings are still stepping down as Elliott Hill clears excess classic inventory and absorbs Q1 FY2027's 26% constant-currency plunge in Greater China.

Let's run the Reverse DCF together so we know exactly what a buyer at $37.99 is signing up for. Using a 9.0% discount rate and a 3.0% terminal growth rate, $37.99 is not priced for doom. It already bakes in 3.5% annual revenue growth for the next decade and an operating margin recovery from 8.2% (6.0% ex-tariff recovery) all the way back to 11.5%. If NIKE only manages 1.5% growth and an 8.5% margin, the math says fair value sits closer to $28 a share. To earn a genuine margin of safety and push toward $45 to $60, NIKE has to deliver 4.5% to 6.0% top-line growth and 12.5%+ operating margins.

And then look across the aisle at the peer table. That is where the valuation gut-check gets really interesting. Deckers—the parent of HOKA, one of the very brands eating into NIKE's performance running share—earns a 23.5% operating margin and a 38.1% return on invested capital, yet trades at 10.7x forward earnings. On Holding is growing revenue 24% year-over-year at a 66.7% gross margin and trades at 16.5x forward earnings. Even Lululemon trades at 12.6x forward earnings with an 18.0% operating margin. Paying 25.5x forward earnings for NIKE today means you are paying a hefty turnaround premium over faster-growing, higher-margin competitors solely on the faith that the Swoosh will reclaim its throne.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: The hardest trap in investing is confusing a falling stock price with a cheap valuation. A stock down 45% from its 52-week high can still be expensive if forward earnings are shrinking faster than the share price—and if the dividend ($2.41B) is outpacing free cash flow ($2.18B).

book_subsections.title: The Dividend & Capital Allocation Tension at $37.99
paragraphs: Walk through the cash-flow math with me one more time, because it matters directly to valuation. At $37.99, NIKE's $1.64 trailing annual dividend yields 4.32%. For income-oriented investors, a 4.3% yield from a Dow 30 blue chip looks tempting. Yet in FY2026, NIKE paid out $2.41 billion in dividends against $2.18 billion in free cash flow—a 110% FCF payout ratio.

Can NIKE afford that dividend in the short run thanks to its $9.03 billion cash and short-term investment pile? Yes, for a couple of years. But a company whose dividend consumes more than 100% of free cash flow cannot simultaneously fund heavy brand marketing, retail store refreshes, and aggressive share buybacks without eating into its net cash cushion. Until free cash flow climbs back above $3.5 billion—which requires gross margins recovering toward 45%+ and working capital normalizing—the 4.3% yield is a bridge, not a self-funding compounding engine.

book_subsections.title: Why Comparing NIKE to Deckers and On Holding Changes Everything
paragraphs: Imagine you have $10,000 to allocate to global athletic footwear today, and you place NIKE, Deckers, and On Holding side by side on the desk. Deckers is earning 38.1% return on invested capital with a 23.5% operating margin, yet the market is asking you to pay 10.7x forward earnings. On Holding is compounding its top line at 24% a year with a 66.7% gross margin and asks 16.5x forward earnings. NIKE, meanwhile, is contracting on the top line, earning an 8.8% trailing operating margin, and still asks 25.5x forward earnings.

That comparison is the single clearest antidote to brand nostalgia. You do not need to dislike NIKE's products or doubt its cultural permanence to recognize that at $37.99, the market is already giving NIKE substantial credit for a margin recovery it has not yet delivered. If you demand a margin of safety on turnaround risk, you must either buy NIKE at a lower price where forward multiples compress, or wait until margin expansion proves the denominator is rising.

Even Lululemon—a brand wrestling with its own North American maturation—trades at 12.6x forward earnings with an 18.0% operating margin and 21.6% ROIC. When three direct competitors generate superior margins and higher returns on capital at half of NIKE's forward multiple, discipline demands patience before committing fresh capital.
